title: The Pledges of Aqabah
subtitle: The Ambassador Mus'ab, the Awakening of Yathrib, and the Sovereign Covenant
summary: The First Pledge of Aqabah and its ethical commitments, Mus'ab ibn Umayr's transformative mission as the first ambassador of Islam, the conversion of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, the Second Pledge of Aqabah with seventy-five representatives, the appointment of the twelve leaders, and the birth of a sovereign sanctuary.

sections.text: In the twelfth year of Prophethood (621 CE), the seeds planted at Mina bore abundant fruit. During the pilgrimage season, twelve men from Yathrib—ten from the Khazraj and two from the Aws—arrived in Makkah to meet the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at Al-Aqabah. This historic gathering was the First Pledge of Aqabah, traditionally known as the 'Pledge of Faith' or 'Pledge of Women' (Bay'at al-Nisa') because it established moral and spiritual obligations without military commitments.

As recorded by Imam al-Bukhari in the narration of Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who was among the participants, the Prophet took their oath upon fundamental spiritual and ethical tenets: to worship God alone and associate nothing with Him, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children, not to utter slander intentionally fabricated, and not to disobey in any recognized good. The Prophet declared: 'Whoever among you fulfills this, his reward is with God; and whoever falls short in any of these and is punished in this world, that shall be an expiation for him.'
The starry mountain pass of Aqabah where the covenants of faith were forged.

To nurture this nascent community, the Prophet dispatched a trusted companion as his personal emissary: Mus'ab ibn Umayr. Mus'ab had once been the most elegant, perfumed youth of Makkah, who had renounced a life of aristocratic luxury for the sake of the divine message. Endowed with profound Quranic knowledge, exceptional gentle manners, and diplomatic tact, Mus'ab lodged in Yathrib with As'ad ibn Zurarah.

Mus'ab moved quietly from clan to clan, reciting the Quran and expounding the beauty of monotheism. The turning point arrived when the paramount chieftains of the Aws tribe, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, confronted Mus'ab with spears in hand, furious that he was corrupting their community. Meeting their hostility with serene dignity, Mus'ab said: 'Will you not sit and listen? If you are pleased with what you hear, you may accept it; and if you dislike it, we shall spare you what you abhor.'

Both chieftains agreed, planted their spears in the ground, and listened. As Mus'ab recited the Quran, the radiance of truth transformed their expressions. Both chiefs embraced Islam on that very day. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh returned to his clan, Banu Abd al-Ashhal, and asked: 'How do you view my standing among you?' They replied: 'You are our chieftain and best in judgment.' He declared: 'Then it is unlawful for any man or woman among you to speak to me until you believe in God and His Messenger!' Before evening fell, every member of the clan had entered Islam. By the next pilgrimage season, not a single household of the Ansar remained without Muslims.

In the thirteenth year of Prophethood (622 CE), Mus'ab returned to Makkah leading a delegation of seventy-three men and two women from Yathrib: Nusaybah bint Ka'b (Umm Umarah) and Asma bint Amr (Umm Mani'). They arranged to meet the Prophet secretly at midnight during the Tashriq days at the pass of Al-Aqabah, slipping away from their non-Muslim fellow pilgrims one by one under cover of darkness.

The Prophet ﷺ arrived accompanied by his uncle Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who was not yet a Muslim but wished to ensure his nephew's safety. Al-Abbas addressed the delegates solemnly: 'O people of Khazraj! Muhammad is protected and honored among his clan. If you believe you can fulfill what you pledge and shield him from his adversaries, then bear your responsibility; but if you intend to surrender him after he comes to you, then leave him now!'
The ancient hills surrounding Makkah where seventy-five delegates pledged their lives and loyalty.

Ka'b ibn Malik, who was present, recounted that the delegates replied respectfully: 'We have heard your words; now speak, O Messenger of God, and take for yourself and your Lord whatever you wish.' The Prophet ﷺ recited verses of the Quran, encouraged devotion to God, and stated the terms of the covenant: to listen and obey in ease and hardship, to spend in prosperity and adversity, to enjoin good and forbid evil, to speak the truth for God without fearing the blame of any critic, and to protect him when he arrived in their city as they would protect their own wives and children.

Al-Bara ibn Ma'rur grasped the Prophet's hand and declared with passion: 'Yes, by He who sent you with the truth as a prophet, we shall defend you as we defend our own families! Take our allegiance, O Messenger of God, for by God, we are men of war and masters of armor inherited from generation to generation!'

Abu al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihan then asked with strategic foresight: 'O Messenger of God, there are ties between us and other men—meaning the Jews—which will be severed. If we do this, and God grants you victory, will you return to your people and leave us?' The Prophet ﷺ smiled with radiant warmth and uttered immortal words that sealed their brotherhood forever:

بَلِ الدَّمُ الدَّمُ، وَالْهَدْمُ الْهَدْمُ، أَنَا مِنْكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ مِنِّي، أُحَارِبُ مَنْ حَارَبْتُمْ، وَأُسَالِمُ مَنْ سَالَمْتُمْ
'Nay, blood is blood, and destruction is destruction! I am of you and you are of me; I will fight whom you fight and make peace with whom you make peace.' (Sirat Ibn Hisham & Musnad Ahmad)

The Prophet then instructed them to appoint twelve leaders (Nuqaba')—nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws—to act as guardians of the agreement for their respective clans, mirroring the twelve disciples of Isa. With hands clasping his in fervent commitment, the delegates concluded the Second Pledge of Aqabah. In that midnight hour, Islam ceased to be an embattled underground group; it gained a sovereign homeland, a unified citizenry, and an invincible base of truth.
